theme: God as creator, O LORD, how manifold are your works
settingTheScene: Psalm 104 is one of the longest creation poems in the Bible, and it follows the same order as Genesis 1: light, heavens, waters, earth, vegetation, sun and moon, creatures, humanity. The psalmist appears to be deliberately taking us back through Genesis 1, but as praise rather than narrative. If Genesis 1 is the architect’s blueprint, Psalm 104 is the hymn sung when you walk through the finished house and marvel at the craftsman. Today’s reading covers the first two-thirds, through the work of the day. We will save verses 24-35 for another day in the plan.
observation: The psalm opens with the same call as Psalm 103: “Bless the LORD, O my soul.” This is self-talk, the psalmist commanding his own heart to worship.
God is described as clothed in splendor and majesty, wrapped in light, riding on the clouds. The imagery is regal and cosmic.
The order of creation in this psalm mirrors Genesis 1: light, the firmament, the waters, dry land, vegetation, the heavenly bodies, the creatures.

Notice how much attention is given to water, springs gushing, rivers running, animals drinking. Water is life in the ancient Near East, and the psalmist sees it everywhere as evidence of God’s provision.
Verses 19-23 take the same heavenly bodies that Genesis 1 calls “lights” and shows them at work: the moon marks seasons, the sun governs the rhythm of work and rest for both humans and animals.
Even the lions are seen as “seeking their food from God”, predators included in the picture of God’s provision.
interpretation:
Psalm 104 is what creation theology looks like when it is set on fire. The same God who, in Genesis 1, simply spoke and reality obeyed, is here described in vivid, sensory language. He wraps himself in light as a garment. He stretches out the heavens like a tent. He makes the clouds his chariot and walks on the wings of the wind. The psalm is not just telling us that God made creation; it is showing us that God is intimately involved with every part of it.

This is a crucial corrective to a common misunderstanding. Many people, even Christians, drift toward a kind of deism, the idea that God created the world like a watchmaker, wound it up, and now stands back to watch it run. Psalm 104 refuses that picture. God is not absent from his creation. He is sustaining it moment by moment. The springs in the valleys are flowing right now because God makes them flow. The grass grows for the cattle because God makes it grow. The young lions roar because God provides their food. Every animal you have ever seen drink from a stream is participating in the providence of God.

The structure of the psalm mirrors Genesis 1 deliberately. The same order, light first, then heavens, then waters, then dry land, then vegetation, then heavenly bodies, then animal life, but where Genesis tells you what God did, Psalm 104 tells you that God is still doing it. The verbs are present tense. He is making the wind his messenger right now. He is covering the earth with the deep right now. He is making springs to gush forth right now. This is the doctrine of providence, that God’s care of his creation did not stop at the end of the sixth day. It continues, every second, in every corner of what he has made.

Verse 23 is especially worth lingering on. After describing the night when the lions hunt, the psalm says: “Man goes out to his work and to his labor until the evening.” Human work is part of the rhythm of creation. The sun rises, animals retreat, humans go out to labor, all of it under God’s ordering. The work you will do today, however mundane, however tiring, is part of the symphony of creation that Psalm 104 is celebrating. You are not interrupting God’s work by going to your job. You are participating in it.

This is the kind of meditation Psalm 104 teaches us. To see creation rightly is to see the Creator behind every part of it. To look at a tree is to see God’s craftsmanship. To feel rain on your face is to feel God’s provision. To hear birds in the morning is to hear what God is feeding right now. The whole world becomes a sanctuary when you read it through this psalm.
connection: The first three days of this plan walked through Genesis 1 to 3. Yesterday we let David teach us how to respond to the creation account with Psalm 8, the dignity of humanity. Today the psalmist takes us deeper into the wonder of creation itself. Tomorrow we will return to narrative as Genesis continues. The Psalms are not interruptions to the story; they are the heart’s response to the story. As the plan unfolds, watch how the Psalms keep reframing what we have just read in the language of prayer, lament, and praise. The Bible is not just telling you about God; it is teaching you how to talk back to him.
application:
Today, take Psalm 104 with you. As you go through your day, practice what the psalmist practices: noticing God’s hand in what would normally be background. The water from your tap. The food on your plate. The light in the sky. The wind in the trees. The birds you hear. None of these are accidents. All of them are God’s ongoing creative care, sustained moment by moment by his word.

If you have time, take a short walk outside today and let Psalm 104 shape your eyes. Notice five things you might normally walk past, and silently thank God for each. The point is not to feel mystical, the point is to recover sight. We live in a world that has trained us to see creation as raw material, as background, as something we use. Psalm 104 trains us to see it as a hymn we are walking through. Recovering this vision changes how you treat your food, your body, your environment, and your neighbor. Worship begins with seeing.
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 104:1-23 slowly, twice. This psalm retells the creation story as praise. As you read, see if you can match its verses to the days of Genesis 1, and notice how God is pictured as providing for every creature, from the wild goats to the lions to the people who work the land.
prayerPrompts: Bless the LORD for something you can see or touch right now that he is sustaining.
Ask him to help you receive today’s work and meals as gifts and not as entitlements.
Tell him what it would mean to walk through this day as through a temple.
